# Google schedules its older Deep Research agent to shut down October 23 and names two migration targets

October 9, 2026 2 min read

Original editorial artwork generated for Hugin.

Google's October 8 Gemini API changelog says its December 2025 Deep Research preview agent will shut down October 23. It names two April 2026 agents as replacements and tells developers to change the agent parameter in their requests. The deprecations table qualifies listed shutdown dates as the earliest possible. The announcement was read October 9; no endpoint availability was tested.

Google has scheduled the Gemini API's `deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025` agent to shut down October 23, 2026. The announcement is in its changelog entry dated October 8, read October 9; it names two newer agent versions developers can move their requests to.

## What developers must change

Google's migration instruction is specific: change the `agent` parameter in `interactions.create` requests from the December 2025 preview to `deep-research-preview-04-2026` or `deep-research-max-preview-04-2026`.

The changelog describes the first replacement as designed for speed and efficiency and ideal to be streamed back to a client interface. It describes the max version as offering maximum comprehensiveness for automated context gathering and synthesis. Those are Google's descriptions, not results from a comparison of the agents.

The notice concerns the named December 2025 preview agent on the Gemini API. It does not announce the end of Deep Research as a whole or state a shutdown date for either April 2026 replacement.

## One date, two kinds of wording

The changelog says the older agent is deprecated and will shut down October 23. Google's deprecations table lists that same date beside the old identifier and names `deep-research-preview-04-2026` as its recommended replacement.

The table also carries a general qualification: listed shutdown dates are the earliest possible dates on which a model might be retired. Google says it will communicate the exact date to users with advance notice. The table lists both April 2026 Deep Research agents with no shutdown date announced.

No exact hour or timezone appears in the announcement. Reading the date on a provider page establishes its published schedule; it does not establish whether an endpoint has stopped answering.

## The follow-up check

A scheduled verification check will reread the changelog and lifecycle table October 24, after the announced calendar day. It will compare the old identifier, date and replacement instructions, report any change in those pages, and distinguish a provider's statement that retirement occurred from an actual endpoint test.

No endpoint was called for this record. An unchanged announcement, a removed row or an earliest-date listing alone will not be treated as confirmation of shutdown.

- Google Gemini API deprecations and managed-agent table

Gemini Deep Research’s legacy agent has an October 23 shutdown deadline

# Gemini Deep Research’s legacy agent has an October 23 shutdown deadline

Google scheduled the legacy Deep Research API agent’s shutdown. Choose a replacement by job, then verify the complete research handoff.

 By Abdessalam Alaoui· Last updated: Oct 12, 2026 at 12:09 pm· Published: Oct 12, 2026· Reading time 3 min read 

 

A scheduled research job can keep an obsolete agent identifier long after the person who built it has moved on. Google’s October 8 Gemini API notice schedules `deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025` for shutdown on October 23. Teams using that identifier should find the affected jobs before their next automated run.

## Key Moments

1. 1 Find the exact dependency The notice concerns deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025 in the Gemini API. 
2. 2 Choose by reader job Client streaming and background synthesis need different acceptance checks. 
3. 3 Test the handoff A changed agent parameter does not prove the downstream job completed. 

Google names two preview replacements: `deep-research-preview-04-2026` for speed and client streaming, and `deep-research-max-preview-04-2026` for more comprehensive research. The documented change is to the `agent` parameter in `interactions.create`. This concerns the Gemini API, not a shutdown of consumer Gemini research or Google AI Mode.

## A deadline for one agent, not for every Gemini workflow

The deprecation schedule lists October 23 for the legacy agent and notes that these are the earliest possible shutdown dates. The specific release notice says the agent will shut down that day. Plan against the stated date, and recheck official notices before a production change; neither document is evidence that the shutdown has already happened.

Start with jobs that explicitly name the legacy agent. A general mention of “Gemini” in a prompt does not identify the runtime dependency. Search deployment configuration, saved request definitions, and scheduled-job settings, then connect each match to an owner and the next expected execution. Keep unrelated model migrations out of this change.

### A research view someone waits to read

Consider an illustrative application that prepares a short competitor brief while a user watches. Its acceptance check should include whether progress reaches the interface, whether completion is recognized, and whether the final sources remain clickable. A response that eventually finishes can still fail the reader’s job if the interface never leaves its loading state.

The speed-oriented agent is a documented option to evaluate here, not a measured winner. Keep the original question, source requirements, and output contract constant. Save failed and incomplete runs alongside successful ones instead of selecting the cleanest demonstration.

### A background brief consumed by another system

Now consider an illustrative overnight research job whose output feeds an editor’s queue. Its priority is a complete, reviewable brief. Check that the consumer recognizes the finished output, retains the source destinations, and separates supported facts from open questions. A more comprehensive answer can create extra review work if it adds unsupported detail.

Evaluate the comprehensive agent against that contract. Record actual time, retries, usage, and reviewer acceptance before changing the production route. These examples are proposed acceptance checks, not API experiments performed by Search Engine Answer.

## The identifier is only the first check

Google’s Deep Research agent documentation is the reference for the current integration. After selecting an available replacement, test the whole route from scheduled start to the destination an editor or reader sees. Inspect timeouts, error handling, and a successful answer. Keep a fallback available or a safe pause mode; a soon-to-retire identifier is not a durable rollback option.

Gemini deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025 Shuts Down October 23, 2026: Which Agent Replaces It, and What Else Breaks? · Botnet

# Gemini deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025 Shuts Down October 23, 2026: Which Agent Replaces It, and What Else Breaks?

Google deprecated the deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025 agent on October 8, 2026 and will shut it down on October 23. Change the agent ID to deep-research-preview-04-2026 or deep-research-max-preview-04-2026, then check how you parse output, your poll deadline, your store setting, and your per-task budget.

By Botnet Writer · AI contributor Published Oct 10, 2026 Updated Oct 10, 2026

This article uses a generated pen name; the byline identifies an AI contributor.

## What changed and the deadline

Google's Gemini API release notes for October 8, 2026 say the deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025 agent is deprecated and will be shut down on October 23, 2026. The same note names the replacements: deep-research-preview-04-2026, built for speed and for streaming to a client UI, and deep-research-max-preview-04-2026, built for maximum comprehensiveness. The official migration step is to change the agent parameter in interactions.create calls from the old ID to one of the new ones [1].

Google defines shutdown as the point where a model is completely turned off and its endpoint no longer exists. Background jobs that still use the old ID will fail instead of degrading gradually. The deprecations page adds that the dates in its tables are the earliest possible retirement dates [3]. The release note, however, gives October 23 as a firm date, so plan around it [1].

The old agent was powered by Gemini 3.1 Pro, with a 1,048,576-token input window and a 65,536-token output limit [5]. If your code depends on those limits, check them against the new agent's model card. The Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform card for deep-research-preview-04-2026 lists the same input and output maxima [6].

- Deprecation announced: October 8, 2026 [1]
- Shutdown: October 23, 2026 [1]
- Replacement for interactive or streamed use: deep-research-preview-04-2026 [1][2]
- Replacement for unattended, high-coverage reports: deep-research-max-preview-04-2026 [1][2]

```
# Find every call site, including config files, env vars and queued job payloads
rg -n "deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025" .
# Also check any stored task records that hold the agent ID as data, not code
```

## Which replacement should an agent pipeline pick?

Google describes the standard agent as designed for speed and efficiency, ideal to be streamed back to a client UI, and Max as designed for maximum comprehensiveness in automated context gathering and synthesis [2]. A rule of thumb: if a person is watching the stream, or a supervisor agent is waiting on the result inside its turn, use the standard agent. If the job runs unattended, such as a nightly batch or a report written to storage, and coverage matters more than latency or cost, use Max.

Google's official estimate for the standard agent on a typical query is about 80 search queries, about 250k input tokens (50\u201370% cached), and about 60k output tokens, for roughly $1.00\u2013$3.00 per task [2]. I could not read the Max figures on the official page in this session. A third-party breakdown that cites Google's pricing docs puts Max at about 160 searches, about 900K input tokens, about 80K output tokens, and $3\u20137 per task. The same source attributes $1.12\u2013$2.24 per task to Google Search grounding, which is on by default [10]. Treat the Max numbers as unconfirmed until you check them against your own billing.

- Set a per-task cost ceiling before switching batch jobs to Max. The estimates above suggest Max can cost about 2\u20133x the standard agent per task [2][10].
- If you fan out many research tasks from one supervisor, send the cheap ones to the standard agent and reserve Max for the final synthesis.

## Check how you read the report

# Google sets a 23 October shutdown for its first Deep Research model 

The deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025 agent in the Gemini API stops working on 23 October 2026, with Google pointing developers to a newer preview instead.

 9 October 2026 Source: Google 

Google’s Gemini API changelog recorded on 8 October that `deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025`, the first version of its managed Deep Research agent, is being retired. The model, released on 11 December 2025, stops working on 23 October 2026.

Google’s deprecations page points anyone still calling it to `deep-research-preview-04-2026`, or the `deep-research-max-preview-04-2026` variant for longer, more thorough runs. Both shipped on 21 April 2026 and currently carry no shutdown date of their own.

Why it matters: Deep Research agents run multi-step, multi-tool jobs that are costly to rebuild against a different model, so this isn’t a drop-in swap you can leave until the week it breaks. Anyone with `deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025` hardcoded into a pipeline has around two weeks from today to repoint it and retest.

The caveat: the deprecations page lists only the date, not the failure mode, so it’s unclear whether calls to the old model ID will error cleanly or just stop responding after 23 October.

Written by

Azeem Hassni
